p.src: Now, when Lady Wang heard that Lady Xing had arrived, she hurried out to meet her. Lady Xing still did not know that Grandmother Jia had learned of the affair concerning Yuanyang and had come precisely to inquire what had happened. As soon as she entered the courtyard, however, several old serving women quietly informed her, and only then did she understand. She was about to turn back, but those inside already knew she was there, and Lady Wang had come out to receive her; she therefore had no choice but to enter and first pay her respects to Grandmother Jia. Grandmother Jia did not say a single word, and Lady Xing herself felt ashamed and remorseful. Xifeng had already found some pretext to withdraw. Yuanyang, too, had returned to her room in anger. Aunt Xue, Lady Wang, and the others, fearing that their presence might embarrass Lady Xing, gradually withdrew as well. Lady Xing, however, did not yet dare to leave.

p.src: When Grandmother Jia saw that no one else remained, she said, “I hear you have been acting as matchmaker for your husband. You certainly observe the Three Obediences and Four Virtues—but you carry this wifely goodness altogether too far! Now that sons and grandsons fill your sight, are you still so afraid of him that you cannot even offer a word or two of advice, but must let your husband carry on however his temper dictates?” Lady Xing’s face flushed crimson. “I tried to dissuade him several times,” she replied, “but he would not listen. Is there anything you do not understand, Madam? I had no choice myself.” Grandmother Jia said, “If he forced you to murder someone, would you go and do that too? Think about it now. Your younger brother’s wife is honest by nature and is forever afflicted with one illness or another; is there anyone or anything in this household, high or low, that she does not have to worry about? Though your daughter-in-law helps her, she is forever dropping the rake to pick up the broom, rushing from one task to the next. As for all my own affairs, I have already reduced them as much as I can. Whenever those two overlook something, there is Yuanyang. That child is more attentive: she keeps some thought for my affairs, comes when she ought to be here, and, when anything needs replenishing, finds a suitable moment to tell them to supply it. If Yuanyang did not do all this, how could those two women, with everything inside and outside, great and small, help overlooking a thing or two? Am I to take all the worry back upon myself now? Or must I spend every day reckoning what I need and asking you all for it? Of all the maids in my rooms, capable or otherwise, she alone remains. She is somewhat older now and knows something of all my moods and ways. Besides, she is in favor with her mistresses. She does not rely on me or this lady here for her clothes, nor does she go asking that young mistress for money. That is why, in all the affairs of these past few years, whatever she has said has been trusted by everyone—from your younger sister-in-law and your own daughter-in-law down to every person in the household, great and small. So it is not only I who depend upon her; your younger sister-in-law and your daughter-in-law are spared much worry as well. With such a person beside me, even when my daughters-in-law or granddaughters-in-law fail to think of something, I never go without, and I have no cause to lose my temper. If she leaves now, what sort of person will you find for me to employ? Even if you found someone as precious as a pearl, she would be useless if she did not know how to speak and conduct herself. I was just about to send someone to speak to your husband. Whatever kind of woman he wants, I have the money here; let him freely pay ten or twenty thousand for one if he likes—but he cannot have this maid. Letting her remain and serve me for a few more years will count as though he himself had waited upon me day and night and fully performed his filial duty. You have arrived at just the right time. It will be more fitting if you go and tell him yourself.”

p.src: When she had finished, she summoned a servant and ordered, “Ask Aunt Xue and all you young ladies to come back and talk awhile. We had only just begun enjoying ourselves—why has everyone dispersed again?” The maids promptly assented and went. Everyone hurried back at once. Only Aunt Xue said to the maid, “I have only just been there. What should I go back for? Just tell her that I have gone to sleep.” “Oh, my dear, dear Aunt,” pleaded the maid, “my venerable aunt! Our old mistress is angry, and if you do not go, there will be no calming matters down. Please come, if only out of kindness to us. If you are tired, I will carry you there on my back.” “You little imp,” said Aunt Xue, “what are you so afraid of? At worst she will scold you for a few moments, and then it will be over.” Even as she spoke, she had no choice but to return with the little maid. Grandmother Jia promptly invited her to sit and said with a smile, “Let us play cards. Aunt Xue is out of practice, so let us sit together and not allow Xifeng to muddle our play.” “Quite right,” Aunt Xue replied with a smile. “You must keep an eye on things for me, Madam. Shall just the four of us women play, or should we add someone else?” Lady Wang said with a smile, “Surely there are more than four of us.” “It will be livelier if we add another player,” said Xifeng. “Call Yuanyang,” said Grandmother Jia, “and have her sit below me here. Aunt Xue’s eyesight is failing, so Yuanyang can keep watch over both her cards and mine.” Xifeng heaved a sigh and said to Tanchun, “For all your learning and literacy, it is a pity you never studied fortune-telling!” “What a strange thing to say,” replied Tanchun. Instead of rousing yourself to win a little money from Grandmother, why are you suddenly thinking about fortune-telling?” “I want my fortune told precisely to find out how much I am destined to lose today,” said Xifeng. “As if I could still hope to win! Just look: before I have even entered the field, ambushes have already been laid on both sides.” Her words made both Grandmother Jia and Aunt Xue burst out laughing.

p.src: Before long, Yuanyang arrived and sat below Grandmother Jia, with Xifeng taking the place below her. A red felt cloth was spread out, the tiles were shuffled and the dealer determined, and the five of them drew their hands. After they had played for a while, Yuanyang saw that Grandmother Jia's hand was all but complete and needed only the two of circles, so she secretly signalled Xifeng. It was Xifeng's turn to discard. She deliberately hesitated for some time, then said with a smile, “Aunt must surely be holding back the tile I need. If I don't play this one, I simply can't hold out any longer.” Aunt Xue said, “I have none of the tiles you need.” “I'll inspect your hand afterwards,” said Xifeng. “Inspect it all you like,” said Aunt Xue. Play your tile first and let me see what it is.” Xifeng placed it before Aunt Xue. Seeing that it was the two of circles, Aunt Xue laughed and said, “I have no particular use for it, but I fear the Old Lady has completed her hand.” At this, Xifeng hurriedly laughed and said, “I played the wrong tile.” Grandmother Jia had already thrown down her tiles in delight. “Just try taking it back!” she said. Who told you to make a mistake?” Xifeng said, “It seems I ought to have my fortune told. I brought this trap upon myself, so I have only myself to blame!” “Quite so,” Grandmother Jia replied with a laugh. “You ought to slap that mouth of yours and ask yourself why you did it.” Then she turned to Aunt Xue and said with a smile, “It isn't that I'm stingy or fond of winning money; I merely want the good omen.” Aunt Xue laughed. “Of course. What muddle-headed person would ever say that the Old Lady cared about money?” Xifeng was counting out the coins, but at these words she hurriedly threaded them back onto the string and said to the others with a smile, “That's enough from me. So we truly aren't playing to win money, only to win a lucky omen. I am the stingy one after all, counting my money the moment I lose. Hurry and put it away.” It was Grandmother Jia's custom to have Yuanyang shuffle for her. Engrossed in chatting and joking with Aunt Xue, she failed to see Yuanyang begin, and said, “Why are you sulking? You won't even shuffle the tiles for me.” Yuanyang picked up the tiles and said with a laugh, “Second Mistress hasn't paid.” Grandmother Jia said, “If she won't pay, her luck has turned.” She then ordered a young maid, “Bring me that whole string of hers.” The young maid really did take it and set it beside Grandmother Jia. Xifeng laughed. “Give it to me as a reward, and I'll repay the full amount.” Aunt Xue laughed. “Xifeng really is stingy. It's only a game.” At this, Xifeng rose, took Aunt Xue by the hand, and pointed back at a little wooden cashbox in which Grandmother Jia usually kept money. “Look, Aunt,” she said with a laugh. “Who knows how much of my money has been played into that box? This one string won't last half an hour before the money in that box beckons it over.

p.src: As soon as this string has been called inside as well, there'll be no need to play any more, our Old Ancestress's temper will have subsided, and she'll send me off to attend to some proper business.” Before she had finished, Grandmother Jia and all the others were laughing without cease. Just then, Ping'er, afraid that the money might not suffice, brought over another string. Xifeng said, “Don't put it before me; place it over there with the Old Lady's money. It will save trouble if they're both called inside together. Then the money in the box won't have to do the job twice.” Grandmother Jia laughed so hard that the tiles in her hands scattered all over the table. Pushing Yuanyang forward, she cried, “Quick, tear that mouth of hers!”

p.src: Ping'er set down the money as instructed, joined in the laughter for a while, and then went back. At the courtyard gate she met Jia Lian, who asked her, “Where is Madam? Master has told me to fetch her.” Ping'er hurriedly replied with a smile, “She's with the Old Lady. She's been standing there all this time and hasn't yet left. You had better drop the matter while you can. The Old Lady was angry for half the day, and it was only thanks to Second Mistress amusing her all this while that she has finally calmed down a little.” Jia Lian said, “I'll go in on the pretext of asking the Old Lady whether she intends to visit the Lai household on the fourteenth, so that the sedan chairs can be made ready. That way I can fetch Madam and help cheer her up at the same time. Wouldn't that be best?” Ping'er said with a smile, “If you ask me, you had better not go at all. The whole household, including Madam and Baoyu, has been found at fault, and now you mean to go and add yourself to the list.” Jia Lian said, “It's already over. Surely she won't rake it all up again? Besides, it had nothing to do with me. And what's more, Master personally ordered me to fetch Madam. If I send someone else now and he should find out, he is already in a foul temper and might seize on that as an excuse to vent his anger on me.” With that, he set off. Ping'er saw that his reasoning was sound and followed him.

p.src: When Jia Lian reached the main hall, he softened his steps and peered into the inner room, where he saw Lady Xing standing. Sharp-eyed Xifeng saw him first and signaled that he was not to come in, then gave Lady Xing another meaningful look. Lady Xing could not very well leave at once, so she poured a bowl of tea and set it before Grandmother Jia. When Grandmother Jia turned around, Jia Lian was caught unawares and failed to hide quickly enough. Grandmother Jia asked, “Who is that outside? It looked like some young fellow poking his head in.” Xifeng hurriedly rose and said, “I thought I glimpsed someone too. Let me go and see.” As she spoke, she got up and went outside. Jia Lian hastened inside and said with an ingratiating smile, “I came to ask whether Your Ladyship will be going out on the fourteenth, so that the sedan chair may be made ready.” Grandmother Jia said, “If that is all, why did you not come in? Why skulk about like a ghost?” Jia Lian replied with a smile, “I saw Your Ladyship playing cards and dared not disturb you. I only meant to call my wife out and ask her.” Grandmother Jia said, “Was it so urgent that it had to be this very moment? Once she went home, could you not ask her all you pleased? Since when have you ever been so considerate? Who knows whether you came as a talebearer or a spy? Creeping about like that, you gave me quite a fright. What a thoroughly wretched creature you are! Your wife is playing cards with me, and there is still half a day to spare. Go home and consult that Zhao Er woman again about how to deal with your wife!” At this, everyone laughed. Yuanyang laughed and said, “It was Bao Er’s wife. Our Old Ancestress has dragged Zhao Er’s wife into it again.” Grandmother Jia laughed too. “Quite right! How am I to remember whether it was Bao this or Bei that? Whenever these matters are mentioned, I cannot help getting angry! From the day I entered this household as a great-grandson’s bride until now, when I have a great-grandson’s bride of my own, fifty-four years have passed from beginning to end. I have lived through my share of alarming dangers and every manner of strange event, yet never anything like this. And it happened right here under my own roof!”

Jia Lian said, “It was all Father’s doing, yet now Mother and I have to bear the blame.” Lady Xing said, “You unfilial, heaven-stricken wretch! p.src: In the blink of an eye, the fourteenth arrived, and early that morning Steward Lai’s wife came in once more to extend the invitation. Grandmother Jia was in high spirits and took Lady Wang, Aunt Xue, Baoyu, the young ladies, and the others to spend half the day in Steward Lai’s garden. Though the garden could not compare with Prospect Garden, it was spacious and exceedingly well kept, with springs, rocks, trees, pavilions, towers, and galleries; several of its sights were truly astonishing. In the outer hall were Xue Pan, Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, Jia Rong, and several close kinsmen; more distant relatives had not come, nor had Jia She. The Lai household had also invited several serving officials and a few young men from prominent families to help entertain the guests. Liu Xianglian was among them, and Xue Pan, having met him once before, had never ceased thinking of him. He had also heard that Liu Xianglian loved performing in amateur theatricals, especially romantic plays in the roles of young men and women. Misunderstanding this, he took Liu for a libertine and was eager to cultivate his acquaintance, regretting only that no one had introduced them. Now that chance had brought them together, he was beside himself with delight. Jia Zhen and the others admired Liu’s reputation as well, and once drink had overcome their reserve, they begged him to perform two scenes. After he had finished, they moved their seats beside him and plied him with questions, chatting of this and that.

u.src: In the blink of an eye, the fourteenth arrived, and early that morning Steward Lai’s wife came in once more to extend the invitation.
Grandmother Jia was in high spirits and took Lady Wang, Aunt Xue, Baoyu, the young ladies, and the others to spend half the day in Steward Lai’s garden.

Though the garden could not compare with Prospect Garden, it was spacious and exceedingly well kept, with springs, rocks, trees, pavilions, towers, and galleries; several of its sights were truly astonishing.
In the outer hall were Xue Pan, Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, Jia Rong, and several close kinsmen; more distant relatives had not come, nor had Jia She.
The Lai household had also invited several serving officials and a few young men from prominent families to help entertain the guests.
Liu Xianglian was among them, and Xue Pan, having met him once before, had never ceased thinking of him.

He had also heard that Liu Xianglian loved performing in amateur theatricals, especially romantic plays in the roles of young men and women. Misunderstanding this, he took Liu for a libertine and was eager to cultivate his acquaintance, regretting only that no one had introduced them. Now that chance had brought them together, he was beside himself with delight.
Jia Zhen and the others admired Liu’s reputation as well, and once drink had overcome their reserve, they begged him to perform two scenes.
After he had finished, they moved their seats beside him and plied him with questions, chatting of this and that.

p.src: Liu Xianglian himself came from a distinguished family. He had made nothing of his studies and lost both parents while still young. Frank, chivalrous, and careless of convention by nature, he passionately enjoyed handling spears and swords, gambling and drinking, frequenting courtesans, and playing the flute and zither—there was scarcely anything he would not do. Because he was young and remarkably handsome, those who did not know his background often mistook him for an actor. Steward Lai’s son Lai Shangrong had long been on friendly terms with him, which was why he had invited Liu to help entertain the guests that day. Unexpectedly, after the drinking the others behaved well enough, but Xue Pan alone relapsed into his old ways. Liu Xianglian had long since grown displeased and wanted only an opportunity to slip away and end the matter, but Lai Shangrong stubbornly refused to let him leave. Lai Shangrong also said, “Master Bao asked me about you just now. Though he saw you when he first arrived, there were too many people for him to speak freely. He told me to make sure you did not leave when the gathering ended, because he still has something to say to you. Since you insist on going, wait while I call him out. Once you two have met, you may leave, and it will no longer be my concern.” With that, he ordered the pages to find an old serving woman inside and quietly tell her, “Please ask Master Bao to come out.” The page had been gone less than the time needed to drink a cup of tea when Baoyu duly appeared. Lai Shangrong smiled at Baoyu and said, “Dear uncle, I leave him in your hands. I must go and attend to the guests.” With that, he went straight away.

p.src: Baoyu took Liu Xianglian by the hand and led him into a small study beside the hall, where they sat down. He asked whether Xianglian had visited Qin Zhong's grave during the past few days. “How could I not have gone?” Xianglian replied. “The other day, several of us went out hawking and came within two li of his grave. I thought that, with all the rain we have had this summer, his grave mound might not hold. Without telling the others, I slipped away to look and found that it had indeed shifted a little more. When I returned home, I scraped together a few hundred cash, and early on the third morning I went out, hired two men, and had it properly repaired.” “That explains it,” Baoyu said. “Last month, when the lotus pods ripened in the Prospect Garden pond, I picked ten and sent Mingyan to offer them at his grave. When Mingyan returned, I asked whether the rain had washed the grave away. He said that not only had it not been washed away, but it looked newer than before. I supposed that some of his friends must have rebuilt it. What I hate is being penned up at home every day, unable to decide the least thing for myself. The moment I make a move, someone finds out; one person stops me and another tries to dissuade me. I can talk, but I can do nothing. Even though I have money, I am not free to spend it.” “You need not trouble yourself over that,” Xianglian said. “I am here to attend to things outside; it is enough that you remember him in your heart. The first day of the tenth month is near, and I have already set aside the expenses for visiting his grave. You know I am as poor as a church mouse and have no savings at home. Whenever a little money comes my way, it is gone almost at once. So I thought it best to put this portion aside while I had the chance, lest I find myself empty-handed when the day arrives.” “That was precisely why I meant to send Mingyan to find you,” Baoyu said. “But you are seldom at home. I know you drift about from place to place every day and have no fixed whereabouts.” “There is no need to look for me about this,” Xianglian replied. “Each of us is merely doing what he ought. Besides, I intend to set out again soon and roam the world for three or five years before returning.” At this, Baoyu hastily asked, “Why is that?” Liu Xianglian gave a cold laugh. “You do not know what is on my mind. When the time comes, you will understand for yourself. For now, I must take my leave.” “We have met only with such difficulty,” Baoyu said. “Would it not be better to stay and leave together this evening?” “Your aunt's cousin is still carrying on in the same way,” Xianglian replied. “If I remain, something is bound to happen. It would be better for me to keep out of his way.” Baoyu thought for a moment. “If that is how matters stand, you are right to avoid him. But if you truly intend to travel far away, you must tell me beforehand. Whatever you do, do not leave in secret.” As he spoke, tears began to fall from his eyes. “Of course I shall come to say farewell,” Liu Xianglian said. “Only do not tell anyone else.” With that, he rose to leave and added, “Go back inside. There is no need to see me out.” Still speaking, he left the study.

p.src: He had only just reached the main gate when he encountered Xue Pan, who was already shouting wildly, “Who let young Liu get away?” When Liu Xianglian heard this, sparks of fury seemed to fly from him, and he longed to kill Xue Pan with a single blow. But then he reflected that it would mean striking someone while drunk and that he must also consider Lai Shangrong's reputation, so he forced himself to endure it again and again. Suddenly spotting Xianglian coming out, Xue Pan looked as delighted as if he had found a treasure. Staggering quickly forward, he seized him by the arm and said with a smile, “My dear brother, where have you been?” “I was only taking a walk,” Xianglian replied. “I shall be back shortly.” “My dear brother,” Xue Pan said with a smile, “when you leave, all the fun goes out of the party. Do stay a while, if only for my sake. Whatever urgent business you may have, leave it to your elder brother. There is no need to hurry. With a brother like me, even becoming an official and making your fortune would be easy.” Seeing how disgracefully he was behaving, Xianglian felt both disgusted and humiliated. An idea suddenly occurred to him. He drew Xue Pan aside to a secluded place and asked with a smile, “Is your affection for me sincere, or is it false?” At these words, Xue Pan was so delighted that his heart fairly itched. Casting Xianglian a sidelong glance, he hurriedly said with a smile, “My dear brother, why should you ask me such a thing? If I am not sincere, may I drop dead this very instant!” “If that is so,” Xianglian said, “this is not a convenient place. After we have sat a little longer, I shall leave first. Come out afterward and follow me to my lodgings, and we shall drink together elsewhere all night. I also have two exceptionally fine young companions there who have never yet gone out to entertain anyone. You need not bring even a single attendant. Once you arrive, there will be servants ready to wait upon you.” At this, Xue Pan was so delighted that he instantly sobered by half. “Is that really true?” he asked. “What do you mean?” Xianglian replied. “Here I am treating you with complete sincerity, and still you do not believe me!” Xue Pan hurriedly said with a smile, “I am no fool! How could I possibly disbelieve you? But since I do not know the place, if you go first, where am I to find you?” “My lodgings are outside the north gate,” Xianglian said. “Can you bear to leave home and spend a night beyond the city walls?” Xue Pan laughed. “With you there, what need have I of home?” “In that case,” Xianglian said, “I shall wait for you on the bridge outside the north gate. For now, let us return to the feast and drink. Wait until you see me leave, then come out afterward. That way, they will pay no attention.” Xue Pan heard him and readily agreed. The two then returned to the feast and drank for a while. Xue Pan could scarcely contain himself. He kept watching Xianglian, and the more he dwelt on the prospect, the happier he became. He drained one pot after another without waiting for anyone to urge him, drinking and drinking until, before he knew it, he was eight or nine parts drunk.

p.src: Xianglian rose and slipped out when no one was watching. At the gate he told his page Xingnu, “Go home ahead of me. I shall return after going outside the city.” With that, he mounted his horse, rode straight out through the north gate, and waited for Xue Pan on the bridge. Before the time it would take to eat a meal had passed, Xue Pan appeared in the distance on a large horse, galloping toward him with his mouth agape and eyes bulging, his head swivelling from side to side like a pellet drum. When he rode past Xianglian, he kept staring into the distance and paid no attention to what was close at hand, so he actually went straight past him. Xianglian was both amused and exasperated; he spurred his own horse and followed. As Xue Pan rode on, he saw that the country was becoming increasingly deserted, so he wheeled his horse around to search again. Unexpectedly, the moment he turned he saw Xianglian. Delighted as though he had found a rare treasure, he hurriedly smiled and said, “I knew you were a man who would never break his word.” Xianglian smiled. “Ride on quickly. If someone sees us and follows, it will be awkward.” As he spoke, he spurred ahead, and Xue Pan followed close behind.

p.src: When Xianglian saw that few people now passed that way and that a stretch of reed ponds lay ahead, he dismounted, tethered his horse to a tree, and said to Xue Pan with a smile, “Come down. Let us first swear an oath: if either of us later changes his heart and tells anyone, may the curse of the oath fall upon him.” “That makes sense,” Xue Pan said with a smile. He hurriedly dismounted, tethered his horse to a tree as well, then knelt and declared, “If in time I change my heart and tell anyone, may Heaven strike me and Earth destroy me!” Before he had finished, there came a thump, and the back of his neck felt as though an iron hammer had crashed down upon it. Darkness swept over him and sparks burst before his eyes; unable to control himself, he toppled over. Xianglian stepped forward and looked at him. Knowing him to be a clumsy fellow unused to taking a beating, he had used only a third of his strength. He slapped Xue Pan several times across the face, which instantly swelled and blossomed like a fruit stall. At first Xue Pan struggled to rise, but Xianglian prodded him twice with the toe of his boot and sent him sprawling again. Xue Pan protested, “We were both willing. If you did not want it, you had only to say so. Why lure me out here and beat me?” As he spoke, he poured out a stream of abuse. Xianglian said, “You blind fool! Take a good look and see who Master Liu is! Instead of begging for mercy, you still dare insult me! Killing you would serve no purpose; I shall merely teach you a harsh lesson.” With that, he fetched his riding whip and struck Xue Pan thirty or forty times from his back down to his shins. Most of Xue Pan’s drunkenness had now left him. The pain was unbearable, and he could not help crying, “Ow! Ow!” Xianglian sneered, “Is that all you can bear? I thought you were not afraid of a beating.” As he spoke, he seized Xue Pan by the left leg and dragged him several paces into the mire among the reeds, rolling him until he was covered in muddy water. Then he asked, “Do you recognize me now?” Xue Pan gave no answer but lay face down, groaning. Xianglian threw down the whip and pounded him several times with his fists. Xue Pan rolled about, screaming wildly, “My ribs are broken! I know you are a respectable man. It was only because I mistakenly believed what someone else told me.” “Do not drag anyone else into this,” said Xianglian. “Speak only of what is happening now.” “There is nothing else to say about the present,” said Xue Pan. “You are a respectable man, and I was wrong.” “You must speak more humbly before I spare you,” said Xianglian. Groaning, Xue Pan said, “Dear younger brother.” Xianglian answered with another punch. Xue Pan cried “Ow!” and said, “Dear elder brother.” Xianglian struck him twice more in quick succession. “Ow!” Xue Pan hastily cried. “Dear grandfather, spare this blind fool who could not see whom he was dealing with! From this day onward, I shall respect and fear you.” Xianglian said, “Drink a couple of mouthfuls of that water.”

p.src: Hearing this, Xue Pan frowned and said, “That water is filthy! How can I possibly swallow it?” Xianglian raised his fist to strike him. Xue Pan hurriedly said, “I’ll drink it! I’ll drink it!” Still speaking, he had no choice but to lower his head and take a mouthful from beneath the roots of the reeds. Before he could swallow it, he retched loudly and vomited up everything he had just eaten. “You filthy creature,” said Xianglian. “Eat it all up quickly, and I shall spare you.” At this, Xue Pan repeatedly knocked his head against the ground and pleaded, “Please perform a hidden act of mercy and spare me! I could not eat that even if my life depended on it.” Xianglian said, “The stench is enough to overcome even me.” With that, he abandoned Xue Pan, led his horse away, found the stirrup, and mounted. Only when Xue Pan saw that he had gone did his heart settle. He regretted having so badly mistaken the man. He tried to struggle to his feet, but the pain throughout his body was unbearable.

p.src: Meanwhile, Jia Zhen and the others at the banquet suddenly noticed that both men were missing and searched everywhere without finding them. Someone said, “I think they may have gone out through the north gate.” Xue Pan’s pages habitually feared him, and since he had ordered them not to follow, who among them would have dared to go looking for him? In the end, Jia Zhen remained uneasy and ordered Jia Rong to take the pages and follow every clue. They searched all the way beyond the north gate, and a little more than two li past the bridge they suddenly saw Xue Pan’s horse tethered beside a reed-filled hollow. Everyone exclaimed, “Excellent! Where there is a horse, its rider must be nearby.” They all approached the horse and heard someone groaning among the reeds. They hurried over to look and found Xue Pan with his clothes torn to shreds and his face swollen and split beyond recognition. From head to foot, inside his clothes and out, he had rolled in the mire until he looked like a pig made of mud. Jia Rong had already guessed nine-tenths of what had happened. He hurriedly dismounted and ordered the servants to help Xue Pan out, laughing as he said, “Uncle Xue, you flirt every day, and today you have flirted your way into a reed pit. The Dragon King himself must have fallen for your charms and wanted you for his son-in-law, so you ran headlong into one of his horns.” Xue Pan was so ashamed he wished the earth would open and swallow him. In his condition, how could he possibly mount a horse? Jia Rong therefore had to send someone to the suburb outside the gate to hire a small sedan chair. Xue Pan was seated in it, and they all returned to the city together. Jia Rong still wanted to have him carried to the Lai residence to attend the banquet, but Xue Pan pleaded with him in every possible way and also begged him not to tell anyone. Only then did Jia Rong agree and allow him to return home separately. Jia Rong returned to the Lai residence, reported back to Jia Zhen, and described the scene he had just witnessed. Jia Zhen also understood that Xianglian had beaten him and said with a laugh, “It is just as well that he should suffer a lesson.” When the banquet broke up that evening, he went to inquire after Xue Pan. Xue Pan was recuperating in his bedroom and, claiming illness, refused to see him.

They hurried over to look and found Xue Pan with his clothes torn to shreds and his face swollen and split beyond recognition. From head to foot, inside his clothes and out, he had rolled in the mire until he looked like a pig made of mud.

Jia Rong had already guessed nine-tenths of what had happened. He hurriedly dismounted and ordered the servants to help Xue Pan out, laughing as he said, “Uncle Xue, you flirt every day, and today you have flirted your way into a reed pit.
The Dragon King himself must have fallen for your charms and wanted you for his son-in-law, so you ran headlong into one of his horns.”
Xue Pan was so ashamed he wished the earth would open and swallow him. In his condition, how could he possibly mount a horse?
Jia Rong therefore had to send someone to the suburb outside the gate to hire a small sedan chair. Xue Pan was seated in it, and they all returned to the city together.

Jia Rong still wanted to have him carried to the Lai residence to attend the banquet, but Xue Pan pleaded with him in every possible way and also begged him not to tell anyone. Only then did Jia Rong agree and allow him to return home separately.
Jia Rong returned to the Lai residence, reported back to Jia Zhen, and described the scene he had just witnessed.
Jia Zhen also understood that Xianglian had beaten him and said with a laugh, “It is just as well that he should suffer a lesson.”
When the banquet broke up that evening, he went to inquire after Xue Pan.
Xue Pan was recuperating in his bedroom and, claiming illness, refused to see him.

p.src: When Grandmother Jia and the others returned and went back to their respective quarters, Aunt Xue and Baochai found Xiangling with her eyes swollen from weeping. After asking what had happened, they hurried over to see Xue Pan. Though his face and body bore bruises, neither sinew nor bone had been injured. Aunt Xue was at once distressed and furious. She berated Xue Pan for a while, then Liu Xianglian, and meant to report the matter to Lady Wang and send men to seize Liu Xianglian. Baochai hastily dissuaded her: “This is no great matter. They were merely drinking together, and it is common enough for men to fall out after drinking. Whichever one gets drunker may well take a few extra blows. Besides, everyone knows that our family behaves as though no law in heaven or earth applied to us. Mother only feels this way because your heart aches for him. It will be easy enough to vent your anger. In three or five days, when Brother has recovered and can go out again, Cousin Zhen, Second Cousin Lian, and the rest are hardly likely to let the matter drop. They will naturally arrange a feast, summon that man, and have him apologize and admit his fault before everyone, and that will settle it. But if Mother now makes a great affair of it and tells everyone, it will only make you seem partial and overindulgent—as though you had encouraged him to provoke trouble, yet the moment he happened to come off worse, you raised a great commotion and relied on the power of your relatives to oppress an ordinary man.” Aunt Xue replied, “My dear child, you really do think of everything. Anger clouded my judgment for a moment.” Baochai smiled. “This is for the best. He neither fears Mother nor listens to anyone’s advice, and grows more unruly by the day. After he has suffered two or three such setbacks, perhaps he will finally mend his ways.” Lying on the kang, Xue Pan cursed Liu Xianglian savagely and ordered his pages to tear down Liu’s house, beat him to death, and take the case to court. Aunt Xue restrained the pages, saying only that Liu Xianglian had behaved outrageously while drunk, but that, now sober, he bitterly regretted it and had fled for fear of punishment. When Xue Pan heard this, he wanted to know the truth of the matter. To learn what happened, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
